question: A 25-year-old man with a furuncle of the upper lip (danger area of the face) develops high fever, rigors, bilateral proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and periorbital oedema over 48 hours. CST is confirmed on MRI. Which combination represents the MOST appropriate immediate management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral antibiotics are entirely inadequate for CST — a life-threatening condition with mortality up to 30% even with optimal treatment. IV antibiotics crossing the blood-brain barrier are essential. Nasal decongestants alone do not address the septic thrombosis.

answers.text: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes) + anticoagulation with heparin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. First-line CST management: (1) IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — vancomycin or flucloxacillin (for MRSA/MSSA coverage) + metronidazole (anaerobes) + a third-generation cephalosporin; (2) anticoagulation — LMWH or unfractionated heparin reduces propagation of the septic thrombus and has shown mortality benefit in retrospective studies. Surgical drainage of the primary source (e.g. paranasal sinuses) is added if needed.

answers.text: Systemic corticosteroids alone to reduce orbital inflammation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corticosteroids alone in CST are contraindicated and dangerous — they suppress the immune response while infection propagates. Corticosteroids may be ADDED to antibiotics in selected cases (e.g. pituitary involvement) but are never first-line standalone treatment.

answers.text: Emergency surgical thrombectomy of the cavernous sinus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgical thrombectomy of the cavernous sinus is not feasible given the anatomy — it is a complex dural venous sinus closely related to multiple cranial nerves and the internal carotid artery. Surgery is directed at draining the primary infective focus (e.g. paranasal sinuses, sphenoidal abscess), not at the cavernous sinus itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: CST is a life-threatening condition requiring: (1) IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Staph aureus cover essential — commonest organism); (2) anticoagulation (LMWH/heparin) to prevent thrombus propagation; (3) drainage of primary focus if needed. Oral antibiotics or steroids alone are unsafe.

Correct. IV antibiotics + anticoagulation is the evidence-based standard of care for CST. The route of spread from the 'danger triangle of the face' (upper lip, nose) via the facial vein → angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus is a classic exam pathway.
